newsitem.title: USA: US growth steady, inflation low - NY Fed's McDonough.
newsitem.headline: US growth steady, inflation low - NY Fed's McDonough.

text.p: U.S. economic growth is steady and inflation is low, said Federal Reserve Bank of New York President William McDonough at a breakfast sponsored by the New York City Partnership.
"U.S. growth is steady and moderate and the rate of inflation is low," McDonough told the audience.
As 1997 commences, the U.S. is entering the seventh year of economic expansion, the New York Fed chief said.

Growth seems to be meandering along at a rate of 2.0 to 2.5 percent, McDonough said, adding it it was "Probably well north of that in the fourth quarter of last year, which looks as if it came in quite strong."

McDonough said imbalances no doubt exist in the economy, "But it is difficult for me to see that there are very large ones that would lead you to believe that the pace of growth would either get very high or would drop off to subnormal growth."
McDonough said shocks to the U.S. economy can come from unexpected directions. In Europe, for instance, he noted that first-quarter growth might be slowed by surprisingly severe winter weather.
Still, McDonough said he thinks the risks to the United States economy this year are "reasonably small" and "the prospects of this year therefore are reasonably positive."
McDonough said inflation is always possible, but added that a wage increase "doesn't automatically mean that the United States economy is about to suffer a burst of inflation."
Turning to the regional economy, McDonough said the New York region since the 1991 recession has been doing relatively badly, with job creation in New York and New Jersey below the national level.
"But it is actually getting better. Things I believe are improving," he said. "Thanks to our region's highly integrated market for business and consumer services."

"The prospects for continuing growth in New York City look more solid today than they have in some time," McDonough said He pointed out this year's fiscal difficulties have been softened by taxes paid by the financial services industries.
